He was, in fact, dressed as 'Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,' one of his most impressive characters. The Cantervilles had good reason to remember this performance, since it had actually caused their quarrel with their neighbour, Lord Rufford. It was about quarter past two in the morning, and as far as he could tell, everyone was asleep. He was walking towards the library to check whether anything remained of the bloodstain when two figures suddenly sprang from a dark corner. Waving their arms wildly overhead, they screamed 'BOO!' into his ear.

Naturally terrified under the circumstances, he rushed towards the stairs. But Washington Otis stood waiting there with the large garden syringe. Surrounded by enemies and almost cornered, the ghost vanished into the great iron stove, which fortunately was not burning. He had to crawl home through the smoke passages and chimneys, reaching his room filthy, dishevelled, and full of despair.

After that, nobody saw him on another nighttime outing. The twins waited to ambush him several times and scattered nutshells through the corridors every night, greatly annoying their parents and the servants. Their efforts achieved nothing. Clearly his feelings were so badly hurt that he refused to appear. Mr. Otis therefore returned to his great history of the Democratic Party, on which he had been working for years. Mrs. Otis arranged a magnificent clam bake that astonished the entire county. The boys occupied themselves with lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American national games. Virginia rode her pony along the lanes with the young Duke of Cheshire, who had come to spend the final week of his holiday at Canterville Chase. Everyone generally assumed the ghost had left. Indeed, Mr. Otis wrote to tell Lord Canterville so, and received a reply expressing great pleasure at the news and warm congratulations to the Minister's worthy wife.

The Otises were mistaken, however. The ghost remained in the house and, though now almost too ill to function, had no intention of letting the matter drop. He was especially stirred by hearing that the young Duke of Cheshire was visiting. The Duke's great-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once bet Colonel Carbury a hundred guineas that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost. The next morning he had been discovered on the card-room floor, so helplessly paralysed that, although he lived to a very great age, he could never again say anything except 'Double Sixes.'

At that moment both his eyes and mine caught sight of the scrap of parchment, which I then assumed was paper. It lay half buried in the sand with one corner protruding. Nearby I noticed the remains of a hull that appeared to have belonged to a ship's longboat. The wreck must have been there for an extraordinarily long time, because the wood was barely recognizable as boat timbers.

"Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Soon afterward we started home and encountered Lieutenant G—— along the way. I showed him the insect, and he begged to take it back to the fort. Once I agreed, he immediately slipped it into his waistcoat pocket without the parchment. I had kept that in my hand while he examined the beetle. Perhaps he feared I might change my mind and thought it safest to secure his prize at once—you know how enthusiastic he becomes about anything connected with natural history. Meanwhile, I must have put the parchment into my own pocket without noticing.

"You remember that when I went to the table to draw the beetle, there was no paper in its usual place. I checked the drawer and found none there either. Hoping to discover an old letter, I searched my pockets and came across the parchment. I am explaining precisely how it came into my possession because those circumstances struck me with particular force.

"You will undoubtedly think this fanciful, but I had already recognized a kind of connection. I had joined two links in a much longer chain. There was a boat on a seashore, and close to it lay a piece of parchment—not paper—with a skull drawn upon it. Naturally you will ask, 'What is the connection?' My answer is that a skull, or death's-head, is the familiar emblem of a pirate. Pirates raise the death's-head flag whenever they engage in battle.

"I have emphasized that the fragment was parchment, not paper. Parchment lasts; it is almost indestructible. People rarely record unimportant matters on it, since paper is much better suited to ordinary drawing and writing. That consideration suggested that the skull held some meaning, some relevance. I also paid attention to the parchment's shape. Although an accident of some kind had destroyed one corner, it was clear that the piece had originally been oblong.

The powerful voice—we might call it immaterial, so impossible was it to connect that sound with pipes or keys—fell silent. The girl turned to help her elderly companion and finally noticed us.

He was her father, and since childhood she had guided his blind footsteps. They were Germans from Saxony who had emigrated here only a few years earlier and formed new friendships with the villagers around them. Near the beginning of the plague, a young German student had come to join them. Their simple story was easy to piece together. He was a nobleman in love with the poor musician's beautiful daughter, and he had followed them when they fled the persecution of his friends. But soon the great leveller arrived, its scythe still sharp, to cut down the field's tall flowers along with its grass. The young man was among the first to die. She kept herself alive for her father's sake. Because he was blind, she could maintain a deception that had begun by accident. Now, though they were solitary beings, the land's only survivors, he knew nothing of the change. He did not realize that when he listened to his daughter play, her only other audience consisted of silent mountains, an unfeeling lake, and trees without awareness.

On the very day we arrived, she had developed symptoms of the disease. The thought of leaving her aged, blind father alone on an empty earth filled her with paralysing horror. Yet she could not bring herself to reveal the truth, and the intensity of her desperation drove her to extraordinary efforts. At the usual hour of evening prayer, she brought him to the chapel. Trembling and weeping for his sake, she nevertheless played without a single fault of rhythm or note the hymn celebrating the creation of the beautiful earth that would soon become her grave.

We seemed to her like visitors from heaven. At the appearance of help, her fiercely summoned courage and barely maintained self-control collapsed. She rushed toward us with a scream, clasped Adrian's knees, and could say only, 'Oh, save my father!' Sobs and hysterical cries released the grief she had held back so long.

Poor girl! She and her father now lie together beneath the tall walnut tree where her lover rests, the tree she pointed out to us as she lay dying. At last aware of his daughter's danger, her father could not see the changes in her beloved face. He stubbornly held her hand until death left it cold and stiff. Even then he neither moved nor spoke, until, twelve hours later, merciful death brought him unbroken rest. They lie beneath the grass, with the tree as their monument. That sacred place remains clear in my memory, enclosed by the rugged Jura and the distant, immeasurable Alps. Their church spire still rises among its surrounding trees. Though her hand is cold, I imagine the divine music they loved still drifting there, comforting their gentle spirits.
